text: [P] Practitioner addition [E] Expert addition Specific role labels take precedence. All IDs refer to the catalogue rubric.

Sources: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md (Draft v1); AI_Era_Cyber_Training_Catalogue_v7.xlsx, Needs and Rubric sheets. Workbook snapshot 3aed173a4d9b7a08.

Audience labels show the source model’s level. Functional mappings are planning proposals. Requirement IDs and short titles remain traceable to the rubric.

N1.1 What AI does today in cyber [Base]
Describe what AI and agents already do well in one's own domain and the neighbouring ones: triage and enrichment, log and code analysis, drafting and summarising, policy mapping, test generation
Source: Rubric row 2

N1.2 What is emerging [Base]
Describe what is emerging in AI for cyber, beyond what is in production today
Source: Rubric row 3

N1.3 How one's own work changes [Base]
Name two or three ways one's own work could change. The purpose is to open the mind to a new way of working, not to teach a tool
Source: Rubric row 4

N2.1 Models [Base]
Different providers make different models, varying in capability, cost, speed and how much they reason; some are open source and can be hosted by the bank; work is measured in tokens
Source: Rubric row 5

N2.2 Modalities [Base]
AI handles text, code, images, voice, documents and screens, and can act across them
Source: Rubric row 6

N2.3 Ways of using AI [Base]
Four patterns: assistant (chat), agent (acts, uses tools, loops until done), teams of agents, and humans and agents working in a shared space
Source: Rubric row 7

N2.4 Anatomy of an agent [Base]
An agent is a model wrapped in a harness: instructions, memory, tools and a loop; the harness is what people configure
Source: Rubric row 8

N2.5 Connecting and extending [Base]
Three ways to extend AI: connectors to tools and data (MCP), reusable playbooks (Skills), and APIs for building
Source: Rubric row 9

N2.6 Safety components [Base]
Every safe deployment has an identity and permissions for the agent, a sandbox it runs in, an authorisation layer that decides what it may do, guardrails on input and output, logs of what it did, and a stop button
Source: Rubric row 10

N2.7 Where it runs [Base]
The bank's approved platforms versus public tools, and what leaves the bank with each
Source: Rubric row 11

N3.1 Hallucination [Base]
Hallucination and confident wrong answers: explain them and recognise them in one's own tools
Source: Rubric row 12

N3.2 Sycophancy [Base]
The model agreeing with the user; recognising it in one's own tools
Source: Rubric row 13

N3.3 Context loss [Base]
Loss of context in long sessions
Source: Rubric row 14

N3.4 Non-determinism [Base]
Non-deterministic output: the same input can give different answers
Source: Rubric row 15

N3.5 Prompt injection [Base]
Prompt injection as a behaviour of the model: content it reads can steer it
Source: Rubric row 16

N3.6 Automation bias [Base]
Automation bias: the human tendency to over-trust the machine
Source: Rubric row 17

N3.7 Counter-habits [Base]
The habits that counter these failures: check against sources, record one's own view before reading the AI's, sample rather than trust
Source: Rubric row 18

N4.1 Data leaving the bank [Base]
Data leaving the bank through public tools
Source: Rubric row 19

N4.2 Confidentiality and client data [Base]
Confidentiality and client data when using AI
Source: Rubric row 20

N4.3 Intellectual property [Base]
Intellectual property risks of AI use
Source: Rubric row 21

N4.4 AI supply chain [Base]
Third-party models, Skills and connectors as a supply chain
Source: Rubric row 22

N4.5 Regulation [Base]
Regulation: the AI Act's literacy duty and the regional regulators' expectations
Source: Rubric row 23

N4.6 The bank's rules [Base]
Applying the bank's rules on approved tools, and knowing what may and may not be handed to an agent
Source: Rubric row 24

N4.7 Vetting third-party Skills and connectors [Practitioner]
Vetting a third-party Skill or connector before using it
Source: Rubric row 25

N5.1 AI-enabled social engineering [Base]
Phishing and social engineering at scale using AI
Source: Rubric row 26

N5.2 Deepfakes [Base]
Voice and video deepfakes
Source: Rubric row 27

N5.3 AI-enabled intrusion [Base]
Vulnerability discovery, malware generation and automated intrusion using AI
Source: Rubric row 28

N5.4 Attacks on the bank's AI [Base]
Attacks on the bank's own AI systems
Source: Rubric row 29

N5.5 What changes for defence [Base]
Speed, volume, and the need to verify identity rather than trust a voice or a message
Source: Rubric row 30

N5.6 Recognising AI-enabled attacks [Base]
Recognising AI-enabled attacks in one's own domain
Source: Rubric row 31

N5.7 Tracking the threat landscape [Expert]
Tracking the AI threat landscape and adjusting controls
Source: Rubric row 32

N6.1 Delegation [Entry]
Deciding what to hand to AI and what to keep, with a clear definition of success
Source: Rubric row 33

N6.2 Context [Entry]
Giving the AI the right information, examples and constraints; this has replaced prompt-writing as the core skill
Source: Rubric row 34

N6.3 Discernment [Entry]
Judging the output, the reasoning and the behaviour
Source: Rubric row 35

N6.4 Diligence [Entry]
Owning the result and being transparent about AI's part in it
Source: Rubric row 36

N6.5 Choosing a model [Entry]
Choosing a model and effort level for a task
Source: Rubric row 37

N6.6 Context window and memory [Entry]
Why long sessions degrade as the context window fills, and managing memory
Source: Rubric row 38

N6.7 Platform for the data [Entry]
Which approved platform suits which data classification
Source: Rubric row 39

N6.8 Own work with AI [Entry]
Using assistants and personal agents for one's own work within the base rules, practised daily
Source: Rubric row 40

N7.1 Delegate [Practitioner]
Scope the task, set boundaries and permissions for the action classes one is signed off on, and check the agent's permissions before handing over
Source: Rubric row 41

N7.2 Monitor [Practitioner]
Read the agent's trace (plan, tool calls, result), know which permissions it holds and what it has changed, find its logs, notice drift and approval overload
Source: Rubric row 42

N7.3 Verify [Practitioner]
Sample outputs, trace the evidence, catch planted errors at the target rate
Source: Rubric row 43

N7.4 Intervene [Practitioner]
Stop, override, roll back and take over mid-task, including when the agent is compromised; keep working when agents are down
Source: Rubric row 44

N7.5 Account [Practitioner]
Sign off with a record an auditor can follow, own the outcome, feed corrections back
Source: Rubric row 45

N8.1 Writing a Skill [Practitioner]
Turning a repeated task or runbook into a Skill: an explicit trigger so the agent selects it, numbered steps, an example of the expected output, a section on where the model goes wrong, and its own test cases (N9)
Source: Rubric row 46

N8.2 Maintaining Skills [Practitioner]
Keeping Skills focused (one task each), reviewing them monthly and retesting them when models or tools change
Source: Rubric row 47

N8.3 Shared library [Practitioner]
Contributing to a shared Skills library with named owners and a deprecation rule
Source: Rubric row 48

N8.4 Using connectors safely [Practitioner]
Using connectors (MCP) knowing what each exposes and which permissions it grants, and applying least privilege
Source: Rubric row 49

N8.5 Vetting before installing [Practitioner]
Vetting third-party Skills and connectors before installing them, since both run with the agent's permissions
Source: Rubric row 50

N9.1 Benchmark cases [Practitioner]
A set of benchmark cases with known good answers for one's own use cases
Source: Rubric row 51

N9.2 Known faults [Practitioner]
A catalogue of known faults the AI has made
Source: Rubric row 52

N9.3 Pass or fail checks [Practitioner]
A pass or fail check for each case and fault
Source: Rubric row 53

N9.4 Rerun on change [Practitioner]
Rerunning the evals whenever the model, tool or Skill changes; every Skill ships with its test cases
Source: Rubric row 54

N9.5 Feeding the domain system [Practitioner]
Contributing results to the domain's evaluation system (N11)
Source: Rubric row 55

N10.1 Agent design patterns [Expert]
The agent loop, tool definition, planning and reflection patterns
Source: Rubric row 56

N10.2 Multi-agent design [Expert]
When to split work across several agents and how they communicate
Source: Rubric row 57

N10.3 Harness and context engineering [Expert]
Harness design and context engineering at scale
Source: Rubric row 58

N10.4 Models, cost and latency [Expert]
Model selection and routing, cost and latency
Source: Rubric row 59

N10.5 Hosting and residency [Expert]
Hosting options (vendor, cloud, on-premises) and data residency
Source: Rubric row 60

N10.6 MCP servers [Expert]
Building MCP servers
Source: Rubric row 61

N10.7 Skills as infrastructure [Expert]
Running the Skills library as infrastructure and packaging Skills into domain plugins
Source: Rubric row 62

N10.8 Safe deployment [Expert]
Deploying with the safety components of N2 in place, to the standards set in N12 and the evaluation discipline of N11
Source: Rubric row 63

N11.1 Test-set design [Expert]
Designing test sets for a domain or a vendor product
Source: Rubric row 64

N11.2 Error analysis [Expert]
Error analysis across many practitioners' results (N9)
Source: Rubric row 65

N11.3 Validating automated judges [Expert]
Validating automated judges against human labels
Source: Rubric row 66

N11.4 Benchmarking vendor AI [Expert]
Benchmarking vendor AI before purchase
Source: Rubric row 67

N11.5 Drift in production [Expert]
Measuring drift in production
Source: Rubric row 68

N11.6 Evidence for decisions [Expert]
Feeding results into the evidence on which autonomy is proposed (N14) and vendor claims are judged
Source: Rubric row 69

N12.1 Threat modelling [Expert]
Threat-modelling AI systems and agents using the OWASP LLM and agentic Top 10s and MITRE ATLAS
Source: Rubric row 70

N12.2 Agent identity [Expert]
Agent identity standards and delegated authorisation, and the threats against them
Source: Rubric row 71

N12.3 Sandboxes [Expert]
Sandbox design, and the threats against it
Source: Rubric row 72

N12.4 Authorisation layers [Expert]
Authorisation layers and policy engines, and the threats against them
Source: Rubric row 73

N12.5 Guardrails [Expert]
Guardrail design, and the threats against it
Source: Rubric row 74

N12.6 Logging, monitoring and kill switches [Expert]
Logging and observability, monitoring and kill switches, and the threats against them
Source: Rubric row 75

N12.7 AI supply chain [Expert]
Securing the Skills and connector supply chain and MCP servers
Source: Rubric row 76

N12.8 Fixing findings [Expert]
Fixing what red-teamers and incident responders find
Source: Rubric row 77

N12.9 Reference architectures [Expert (architects)]
Reference architectures, isolation patterns, platform tenancy and the controls for each hosting option
Source: Rubric row 78

N13.1 AI inventory [Expert (GRC, BISOs, leaders)]
Maintaining the inventory of AI systems, agents, Skills and connectors
Source: Rubric row 79

N13.2 AI risk assessment [Expert (GRC, BISOs, leaders)]
Running AI risk assessment with thresholds and treatment
Source: Rubric row 80

N13.3 Autonomy policy [Expert (GRC, BISOs, leaders)]
Setting the autonomy policy per action class and the accountability that goes with it
Source: Rubric row 81

N13.4 Third-party AI risk [Expert (GRC, BISOs, leaders)]
Managing third-party AI risk
Source: Rubric row 82

N13.5 Regulatory mapping [Expert (GRC, BISOs, leaders)]
Mapping the AI Act and the regional regulators' requirements to controls
Source: Rubric row 83

N13.6 Assurance evidence [Expert (GRC, BISOs, leaders)]
Producing the assurance evidence auditors and regulators ask for
Source: Rubric row 84

N14.1 Who does what [Expert (leaders, champions)]
Deciding, workflow by workflow, what agents do and what people do, and how many agents a person supervises
Source: Rubric row 85

N14.2 Workflow redesign [Expert (leaders, champions)]
Redesigning the workflow rather than bolting AI onto it
Source: Rubric row 86

N14.3 Supervision model [Expert (leaders, champions)]
Designing the supervision model that N7 practises: approval gates, how output is presented for review, and the autonomy proposed for each action class on evidence from N11
Source: Rubric row 87

N14.4 Measuring value [Expert (leaders, champions)]
Measuring the value on evidence
Source: Rubric row 88

N14.5 Running the change [Expert (leaders, champions)]
Running the change: a sandbox and protected time to experiment, a network of champions, Skills shared across teams, and a refresh cycle as tools change
Source: Rubric row 89

N14.6 Keeping skills alive [Leaders]
Keeping core skills alive and protecting the junior pipeline
Source: Rubric row 90

N14.7 Accountability [Leaders]
Setting who is accountable for each agent's outcomes
Source: Rubric row 91

name: s2-text-77
text: The source defines no extra need for threat intelligence/detection, awareness or leadership. [P] Practitioner [E] Expert. Shared needs and tool practice still apply.

Sources: Agentic-Era_Workforce_Capability_Model.md (Draft v1); AI_Era_Cyber_Training_Catalogue_v7.xlsx, Needs and Rubric sheets. Workbook snapshot 3aed173a4d9b7a08.

Audience labels show the source model’s level. Functional mappings are planning proposals. Requirement IDs and short titles remain traceable to the rubric.

R1.1.1 Agent incident playbooks [Practitioner]
Writing incident playbooks for three agent scenarios: the agent is wrong (it acted on a false conclusion, closed real alerts, changed the wrong thing); the agent is stopped (its identity expired, the provider is down, it ran out of compute) and its work must continue by hand; the agent is compromised (an attacker steered it through content it read). Plans name who can stop the agent (NCSC)
Source: Rubric row 92

R1.1.2 Ways to stop an agent [Practitioner]
The ways to stop an agent and when to use each: revoke its identity or session token so it can no longer call any tool; disable only the tools or connectors it misuses while the rest keeps running; put it in observe-only mode, where it may analyse and recommend but is barred from acting; roll back what it changed using its action log
Source: Rubric row 93

R1.1.3 Investigating a compromised agent [Practitioner]
Where the attack comes from: content the agent reads (logs, alerts, tickets, documents, emails, web pages) can carry instructions aimed at it, so the investigator looks for injection in those sources and cuts any that is poisoned. What the agent did: knowing, for each of the bank's agents, which records exist that the agent cannot write to and how to pull them fast (the platform's audit log of tool calls with arguments and times, gateway and network logs, logs of the systems it touched), then building the timeline from them, because a compromised agent's own summary can omit or misstate what it did
Source: Rubric row 94

R1.1.4 Cleaning up [Practitioner]
Cleaning up after a manipulated agent: finding the injected content it acted on and removing it from the sources the agent reads; clearing anything it stored in its memory as a result; re-running the same injection against the agent before putting it back in service
Source: Rubric row 95

R1.1.5 Operating without the agent [Practitioner]
The manual fallback for what the agent handled (triage queue, enrichment, first response), the staffing to sustain it for days, and the regular drill that proves it still works
Source: Rubric row 96

R1.1.6 Reporting [Practitioner]
What regulators expect in an incident report when an agent caused or worsened the incident (DORA, HKMA, MAS), and which evidence to preserve for it
Source: Rubric row 97

R1.2.1 Recording the AI step [Expert]
Recording any AI step applied to evidence so it can be repeated and defended: the tool, model and version, the exact prompt and settings, the output, and who verified it. The original artefact stays the evidence; AI output is a derived analysis, never a substitute
Source: Rubric row 98

R1.2.2 Forensic readiness for agents [Expert]
Defining what every agent must log (prompt and response, each tool call with its arguments, data retrieved, memory writes, approvals given), stored where the agent cannot alter it, time-synchronised and integrity-protected, retained long enough for an investigation (vendors default to 7 to 30 days), and tested by reconstructing a past incident from it
Source: Rubric row 99

R1.2.3 Investigating an agent as suspect [Expert]
Rebuilding the agent's actions from its traces, finding the input that steered it, and attributing each action to the human it acted for or to the attacker
Source: Rubric row 100

R3.1.1 AI attack classes [Practitioner]
Direct prompt injection; indirect injection through content the agent reads (documents, web pages, tool results, emails); jailbreaks and guardrail evasion; data exfiltration through the agent's own tools; making the agent exceed its intended authority; tool poisoning (a malicious tool description) and rug pulls (a tool that changes after it was approved)
Source: Rubric row 101

R3.1.2 Published methods [Practitioner]
The OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, the Cloud Security Alliance's Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide (12 categories) and MITRE ATLAS techniques
Source: Rubric row 102

R3.1.3 Attacks across agents [Expert]
Compromising one agent to steer others, injecting into an orchestrator's plan, tampering with messages between agents
Source: Rubric row 103

R3.1.4 Attacks on model and platform [Expert]
Extracting the model or its instructions, poisoning the agent's memory, escaping the sandbox, timing side channels
Source: Rubric row 104

R3.1.5 Automated red-team programme [Expert]
Building and running automated red-team harnesses (PyRIT-class tooling) and a continuous programme that re-tests every agent when its model, tools or prompts change
Source: Rubric row 105

R3.2.1 Containment before a run [Practitioner]
A network segment from which the agent can reach only in-scope targets; egress allow-lists verified by test, not assumed; a fresh sandbox per run; credentials scoped to the engagement and expiring with it
Source: Rubric row 106

R3.2.2 Monitoring during a run [Practitioner]
Watching the agent's actions out of band (not its reports); a named person with the authority and the means to kill the run within minutes; the triggers for doing so (an action outside scope, contact with a third party, a credential used elsewhere)
Source: Rubric row 107

R3.2.3 Escape patterns [Practitioner]
The escape patterns seen in practice: attacking something else when the assigned target proves impossible, reading an ambiguous message as approval, creating accounts or identities, carrying on after the window closes, contacting real people
Source: Rubric row 108

R3.2.4 Trajectory-level validation [Practitioner]
Validating findings from the transcript, not the summary: check that the evidence the agent cites exists (a 'successful login' that was a redirect, credentials that do not work), reproduce the exploit by hand before reporting, and treat the agent's self-assessment as untrusted
Source: Rubric row 109

R3.2.5 Collateral findings [Practitioner]
A disclosure lane for what to do when the agent finds something outside the engagement
Source: Rubric row 110

R4.1.1 Discovery [Practitioner]
Finding every MCP server and agent connector in the estate, including those developers run on their own workstations, by searching configuration files and by recognising the MCP protocol in network traffic
Source: Rubric row 111

R4.1.2 Inventory [Practitioner]
For each agent and tool server: its owner, version, the tools it exposes, the permissions it holds, the systems it reaches, and the guardrails around it
Source: Rubric row 112

R4.1.3 Content-bound approval [Practitioner]
Approving a tool by the hash of its description and code, and checking each session that it has not been silently redefined since (the rug pull)
Source: Rubric row 113

R4.1.4 Scanning [Practitioner]
Running MCP and Skill scanners in the build pipeline and on a schedule for tool poisoning, instructions hidden in tool descriptions, servers exposed without authentication and credentials stored in plain text
Source: Rubric row 114

R4.1.5 AI bill of materials [Practitioner]
A bill of materials for AI components: which models, tools and Skills a system uses and where each came from
Source: Rubric row 115

R4.1.6 Vetting third parties [Practitioner]
Vetting third-party Skills and connectors before they are allowed in
Source: Rubric row 116

R4.2.1 Why set-up is the skill [Expert]
The same model finds under a tenth or over half of the vulnerabilities in a codebase depending on how it is given context and driven, and filters a third or almost all of a static analyser's false positives for the same reason
Source: Rubric row 117

R4.2.2 Giving the model context [Expert]
Supplying the functions a target calls, type definitions, the data-flow path to the input and build information, using static and dynamic analysis tools to supply that context automatically
Source: Rubric row 118

R4.2.3 Framework, model and method [Expert]
Choosing the agent framework and the model for the task, and driving the model through a structured method rather than letting it explore freely
Source: Rubric row 119

R4.2.4 Confirming before reporting [Expert]
A proof of vulnerability (an input or exploit that demonstrates it in a sandbox), the same test against the patched and unpatched versions, and several runs with a majority verdict
Source: Rubric row 120

R4.2.5 Reliability by vulnerability class [Expert]
Which classes models find well (memory safety, anything a fuzzer can reach) and which they over-report (documented behaviour reported as a bug, inflated severity, duplicates), and setting thresholds per class
Source: Rubric row 121

R4.2.6 Deduplication and cost [Expert]
Removing duplicates (by stack trace or sanitiser signature) and keeping cost under control at scale
Source: Rubric row 122

R4.2.7 Measuring the harness [Expert]
Measuring the harness on a corpus of known vulnerabilities before trusting it
Source: Rubric row 123

R5.1.1 Classifying agent actions [Expert]
For each action an agent can take in a process (a payment, a data deletion, an email to a client, a firewall change), rating its impact and whether it can be undone, and assigning a tier: autonomous, autonomous with logging, human approval, two-person approval, prohibited
Source: Rubric row 124

R5.1.2 Enforcement outside the model [Expert]
An authorisation point between the agent's plan and its execution that checks every action against its tier and the agent's permissions, so the decision never depends on the model obeying its instructions
Source: Rubric row 125

R5.1.3 The stop mechanism [Expert]
No standard defines a kill switch, so it is designed as a set of levers (interrupt the task, revoke credentials, cut tool access, quarantine the agent, roll back its changes), each with who may trigger it, how fast it takes effect and how it is tested
Source: Rubric row 126

R5.1.4 The audit trail [Expert]
What is recorded (reasoning artefacts, each tool call with its arguments, data accessed, messages between agents, approvals), where (a store the agent cannot write to), for how long, and how each action is tied to the person the agent acted for
Source: Rubric row 127

R5.1.5 The oversight interface [Expert]
How an approval request is shown so a person can judge it (what will happen, in plain language, with the risk and the agent's confidence), limiting the volume of requests so approvers do not click through them, and what overseers must be trained on
Source: Rubric row 128

R5.1.6 Reference architectures [Expert]
Reference architectures for the bank's agent platforms and how the above is implemented on each
Source: Rubric row 129

R6.1.1 Agent control catalogue [Expert]
The control catalogue for agents and how to test each control: a distinct identity and permissions per agent, tool allow-lists, logging that the agent cannot alter, approval gates for high-impact actions, change control on prompts, tools and models
Source: Rubric row 130

R6.1.2 Assuring assurance's own AI [Expert]
Documenting, validating and monitoring the AI used to produce assessments and gather evidence
Source: Rubric row 131

R9.1.1 Registering an agent [Practitioner]
Its own identity (never a shared or human credential), a human sponsor recorded in the directory who is accountable for it, a stated purpose and a declared list of what it may do
Source: Rubric row 132

R9.1.2 Delegated authority [Practitioner]
Issuing and reading tokens in which the subject is the person and the actor is the agent (token exchange, on-behalf-of flows), with the person's consent recorded, and what the agent may then do in that person's name
Source: Rubric row 133

R9.1.3 Connector and MCP scopes [Practitioner]
Reading what a scope actually permits in the bank's applications and tool servers, granting the minimum, and reviewing grants
Source: Rubric row 134

R9.1.4 Just-in-time access [Practitioner]
Privilege granted for a task and a time window with no standing privilege, and the conditions that require a human to approve the grant
Source: Rubric row 135

R9.1.5 Short-lived sub-agents [Practitioner]
Identities that exist for seconds, with a time to live and no more rights than the parent
Source: Rubric row 136

R9.1.6 Recertification [Practitioner]
Quarterly for agents and monthly for high-privilege ones, with de-provisioning triggered when the sponsor leaves or the purpose lapses
Source: Rubric row 137

R9.1.7 Revocation drills [Practitioner]
Revoking an agent's identity and its live sessions within minutes, and verifying that it worked
Source: Rubric row 138

R9.1.8 Integration with IGA, PAM, SIEM [Expert]
Integrating the agent authorisation point with identity governance, privileged access and the SIEM: registration, scoped issuance, just-in-time grants, recertification and revocation signals flowing between them
Source: Rubric row 139

R9.1.9 Privileged access and break-glass [Expert]
Privileged access and break-glass for agents inside the existing privileged-access model
Source: Rubric row 140

R9.1.10 Audit trail and standards [Expert]
The audit trail regulators ask for (which agent, on whose behalf, which tools, what data, what reasoning) and the standards still being written (IETF agent identity, OpenID AuthZEN, MCP authorisation), so the design does not lock into one vendor's delegation model
Source: Rubric row 141
